newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua finance minister sees economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua finance minister sees economic growth.

text.p: Nicaragua's finance minister on Monday predicted continuing economic growth for this impoverished Central American country, saying Nicaragua will have Latin America's fastest-growing economy in 1997.

"We're growing for the third consecutive year with stability and we are doing it at one of the highest rates in Latin America," Finance Minister Emilio Pereira told the television news program Buenos Dias.

Pereira and other ministers in the government of President Violeta Chamorro will step down on January 10, when Chamorro hands over to President-elect Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance.

Pereira said Nicaragua's gross domestic product of about $2 billion a year will grow by 5.6 percent in 1996 and by seven percent in 1997, which he said would be the highest expected growth rate in Latin America.
He said inflation, expected to be under 10 percent in 1996, will drop to nine percent in 1997.
"After five years of work, I can responsibly say that we are an emerging country, with a future and capacity for growth," Pereira said.
Nicaragua is digging itself out from the collapse of its economy in the 1980s due to a bloody eight-year civil war, a tough U.S. economic embargo and a failed leftist economic policy.
Pereira repeated his assertion that Nicaragua would have to grow by eight percent per year for 15 consecutive years to achieve the per-capita income it had in 1970.

Nicaragua's economic transformation from socialism to the free market began after the 1990 election victory of Chamorro, a centrist who defeated former President Daniel Ortega of the leftist Sandinista Front.

Under Chamorro, Nicaragua has charted a tough, free-market course, cutting spending, reducing inflation and cutting the foreign debt from $12 billion in 1990 to $3.8 billion -- mostly through forgiveness from former Eastern bloc governments but also through debt renegotiation.
Despite three consecutive years of growth and low inflation, more than 70 percent of Nicaraguans live in poverty and 53 percent are unemployed or underemployed.

"It is not enough that the economy grows and inflation drops. We have to transfer this to the majority of the population for Nicaragua to have a future. The challenge for the next government will be social policy," Pereira said. "The new government will not have to seed again, only water the plants left by President Chamorro," he said.
Pereira said the main threat to economic growth lay in populism, and he warned against quick-fix solutions to the problems of low salaries and poor health care and education.
